opinion_question.title: Genocide in Gaza
opinion_question.statement: Between 7 October 2023 and 31 December 2025, Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, as defined by the 1948 Genocide Convention.

scope_note: Occurrence claim within a fixed period, not an assertion that every operation or every phase had genocidal intent. Later publications may provide evidence about the defined period.

facts.prompt: Under the Genocide Convention, what must be established for conduct to constitute genocide?
options: A listed prohibited act committed knowing that severe civilian suffering is likely to result
A listed prohibited act committed with intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part
A campaign of exceptionally destructive violence that kills a large share of the civilian population
A declared intention to destroy a protected group, whether or not a prohibited act is committed
facts.explanation: Article II requires acts and specific group-destructive intent together. Neither intention without a prohibited act nor foreseeable civilian suffering alone establishes completed genocide. The same physical outcome can require different legal classification if the proven intent differs.
facts.source_name: United Nations — Genocide Convention, Article II
facts.importance_rationale: Establishes both necessary elements and distinguishes specific intent from foresight of civilian harm.
facts.gateway_rationale: Establishes both necessary elements and distinguishes specific intent from foresight of civilian harm.
facts.knowledge_rationale: Establishes both necessary elements and distinguishes specific intent from foresight of civilian harm. Prior knowledge requires focused reading on the relevant policy, report or legal distinction.
facts.answerability_rationale: The item tests Article II. The alternatives express credible but substantively different accounts; the source supports one best answer.

facts.prompt: What did Defence Minister Yoav Gallant announce for Gaza on 9 October 2023, as recorded by the ICJ?
options: A weapons embargo while civilian food and fuel deliveries continued normally
A temporary closure of one crossing while all other supply routes stayed open
A restriction on military fuel depots while electricity and civilian supplies were exempted
A complete siege cutting electricity, food and fuel supplies
facts.explanation: The announcement concerned necessities for the population, not only individual military targets. It is evidence of a stated policy by a senior decision-maker. Its implementation, duration, subsequent changes and purpose still require examination; the announcement alone is not a genocide finding.
facts.source_name: International Court of Justice — Order of 26 January 2024, recorded official statements

facts.prompt: What objectives did Netanyahu publicly state for the Gaza war on 6 January 2024?
options: Returning hostages, retaining Hamas as Gaza’s civil administration and withdrawing Israeli forces
Ending Hamas rule, transferring Gaza to the Palestinian Authority and permanently ending Israeli border controls
Occupying northern Gaza, restoring Israeli settlements and leaving Hamas to administer the south
Eliminating Hamas, returning hostages and preventing future threats from Gaza
facts.explanation: These were declared military and security objectives. They are relevant evidence of stated purpose, not conclusive proof of actual intent or lawful methods. Their explanatory value depends on the relationship between declarations, decisions and conduct.

facts.prompt: Which method of destruction is expressly included in Article II of the Genocide Convention?
options: Preventing the group from exercising political autonomy while preserving its physical survival
Deliberately imposing living conditions calculated to bring about the group’s physical destruction
Destroying cultural institutions with the purpose of assimilating the group into a different culture
Compelling the group to relocate while intending its continued physical survival in another place
facts.explanation: Starvation and deprivation can fall within Article II(c) when its conditions and the additional specific intent are established. Genocide need not take the form of direct executions. Political suppression, cultural destruction and displacement require separate legal analysis.
facts.source_name: United Nations — Genocide Convention, Article II
facts.importance_rationale: Makes the survival-conditions allegation legible without equating every deprivation with genocide.

facts.source_locator: WHO release, 6 November 2024, campaign coverage and pauses
facts.prompt: What did WHO report about the second round of Gaza’s polio campaign completed in November 2024?
options: Over 550,000 children received a second dose under local pauses, while some northern areas remained inaccessible
About 550,000 children received a second dose, with full access to the northern areas targeted in the first round
The second round reached central and southern Gaza, but its northern phase was cancelled without any vaccinations
The campaign achieved at least 90% coverage in every community, with no remaining geographical access gaps
facts.explanation: WHO reported 556,774 second doses and estimated that 7,000–10,000 children in inaccessible northern areas remained unvaccinated. The result is concrete humanitarian coordination with substantial reach and real limits, neither universal protection nor a token measure without effect.

facts.prompt: When genocidal intent is inferred from a pattern of conduct, what merits test did the ICJ apply in Croatia v. Serbia?
options: It must be the only reasonable inference from the pattern
It must be more likely than any single competing inference
It must be one credible inference supported by the pattern
It must be the inference supported by the largest number of incidents
facts.explanation: The test is stricter than choosing the most persuasive explanation. A reasonable account without genocidal intent matters; an imagined possibility unsupported by evidence is not automatically reasonable. Failure to establish this inference does not itself prove that genocidal intent was absent.
facts.source_name: International Court of Justice — Summary of judgment, 3 February 2015
facts.importance_rationale: Directly establishes the standard against which the competing-explanation exercise must be assessed.
facts.knowledge_rationale: Directly establishes the standard against which the competing-explanation exercise must be assessed. Prior knowledge requires sustained study of the relevant legal reasoning or evidence method.
facts.answerability_rationale: The item tests Judgment paragraphs 132–148 and 407–440. The alternatives express credible but substantively different accounts; the source supports one best answer.

facts.prompt: What did the ICJ require in its 28 March 2024 Gaza order after warning that famine was setting in?

An immediate unconditional end to all combat throughout Gaza and withdrawal of Israeli forces
Humanitarian deliveries through Rafah only, with other crossing arrangements left unchanged
Expanded humanitarian access conditional on the prior release of all remaining Israeli hostages
facts.explanation: The order supplies a dated, authoritative warning and a requirement for action on food, water, fuel, medical care and other necessities. It is relevant to what officials were on notice about and their subsequent response, not a final finding of genocidal intent or an IPC classification.
facts.source_name: ICJ — order of 28 March 2024

facts.prompt: Under the ICRC’s explanation of targeting law, how is anticipated civilian harm assessed in an attack on a military objective?
options: Against the civilian losses suffered by the attacking state during the original enemy attack
Against the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated, alongside precautionary duties
Against the total strategic benefit of defeating the enemy, regardless of the particular attack
Against the eventual number of enemy fighters killed, using the outcome rather than prior expectations
facts.explanation: Civilian deaths do not alone establish an unlawful attack; a military target does not alone establish a lawful one. Proportionality concerns expected harm and anticipated advantage, with feasible precautions. That targeting assessment is distinct from establishing genocidal intent.
facts.source_name: ICRC — Targeting under international humanitarian law
facts.importance_rationale: Allows a genuine military explanation to be examined without treating all civilian deaths as crimes or all targets as lawful.
facts.gateway_rationale: Allows a genuine military explanation to be examined without treating all civilian deaths as crimes or all targets as lawful.

facts.prompt: According to the ICJ’s genocide case law, how does forced displacement relate to destruction of a protected group?
options: Permanent expulsion is itself the required destruction when the displaced population cannot return home
Expulsion constitutes destruction when it removes a majority of the group from a particular territory
Expulsion and physical or biological destruction are distinct, although displacement can contribute to genocide
Expulsion constitutes destruction when authorities intend to erase the group’s historical connection to its land
facts.explanation: The ICJ distinguishes physical or biological destruction from making an area ethnically homogeneous through removal. Displacement may still be a grave crime and evidence of genocide when the relevant acts and destructive intent are established.
facts.source_name: International Court of Justice — Croatia v. Serbia, 2015 judgment
facts.importance_rationale: Separates removal, an important competing explanation, from the Convention’s destruction requirement.
facts.knowledge_rationale: Separates removal, an important competing explanation, from the Convention’s destruction requirement. Prior knowledge requires sustained study of the relevant legal reasoning or evidence method.
facts.answerability_rationale: The item tests Judgment paragraphs 134–139. The alternatives express credible but substantively different accounts; the source supports one best answer.

facts.prompt: Why did the ICJ reject Croatia’s genocide claim against Serbia in 2015 despite finding killings and serious harm?
options: The killings were too few to reach the Convention’s minimum numerical threshold
The killings were excluded because they occurred during a recognized armed conflict
The victims were not members of a national or ethnic group protected by the Convention
The required specific intent to destroy the Croat group had not been proved
facts.explanation: The Court distinguished prohibited physical acts from the additional destructive intent. Failure to prove genocide did not make the atrocities lawful or establish that no other international crimes occurred.
facts.source_name: International Court of Justice — Croatia v. Serbia case overview
facts.importance_rationale: Shows a real merits dismissal despite atrocities, rather than an assumed classification of a different war.

facts.prompt: What distinction did the Jelisić Appeals Chamber draw between a perpetrator’s motive and genocidal intent?
options: A personal motive can coexist with the specific intent to destroy a protected group
A political motive replaces specific intent when destroying a group serves a wider objective
A financial motive excludes specific intent when the perpetrator principally seeks material gain
A personal motive establishes specific intent when the perpetrator targets people of one ethnicity
facts.explanation: The judgment distinguishes why a perpetrator seeks an outcome from whether group destruction is intended. A further purpose is not automatic disproof of destructive intent, and is not proof of it either. Whether military aims coexist with such intent in Gaza remains an evidential question.
facts.source_name: International tribunal — Jelisić appeal judgment, 5 July 2001
facts.importance_rationale: Explains why an additional objective does not settle whether group destruction was also intended.
facts.knowledge_rationale: Explains why an additional objective does not settle whether group destruction was also intended. Prior knowledge requires sustained study of the relevant legal reasoning or evidence method.

facts.prompt: What new evidence did the Gaza Mortality Survey, published in February 2026, use to estimate deaths through early January 2025?
options: A census of every Gaza household, yielding exactly 75,200 identified civilian deaths
A reclassification of the ministry’s existing death list, yielding 75,200 confirmed combatant and civilian records
A projection from mortality in other wars, yielding 75,200 future direct and indirect deaths
A field survey of 2,000 households, yielding about 75,200 violent deaths with a confidence interval
facts.explanation: The survey estimated 75,200 violent deaths, with a 95% interval of 63,600–86,800. It sampled accessible areas and used weighting to represent the population. It is separate from ministry death enumeration, but missing households, recall and sampling remain limitations. It does not classify combatants or measure events after its study period.

facts.prompt: What qualification did the UN Commission record when discussing Herzog’s October 2023 collective-responsibility statement?
options: He said his reference to national responsibility applied only to people who directly took part on 7 October
He said Gaza’s civilians bore no responsibility and withdrew the collective-responsibility statement
He also acknowledged innocent Palestinians who disagreed with Hamas’s actions
He said his remarks described military-age men alone and explicitly excluded other Gaza residents
facts.explanation: The Commission recorded the qualification but considered it an attempt to deflect responsibility; that interpretation is contested. Both the collective-responsibility language and its qualification belong in the evidence. Neither an isolated phrase nor a later clarification alone settles purpose or operational authority.
facts.source_name: UN Commission of Inquiry — legal analysis, September 2025

facts.prompt: Under the international rules of state responsibility, how is conduct by military units acting as state organs generally treated?
options: As conduct attributable to the state, including when official action exceeds their authority
As conduct attributable to the state only after individual soldiers have been criminally convicted
As private conduct unless the head of government personally approved the particular operation
As private conduct when a military unit violates instructions issued by its political leadership
facts.explanation: Articles 4 and 7 address official conduct by state organs, including action exceeding authority. Attribution is separate from proving the prohibited acts and genocidal intent. A private citizen’s statement and a military unit’s official conduct therefore raise different attribution questions.
facts.source_name: International Law Commission — Articles on State Responsibility
facts.importance_rationale: Connects evidence about actors and authority to the proposition about state responsibility.

facts.prompt: If Hamas unlawfully uses civilians to shield military operations, what happens to Israel’s obligations toward those civilians?

facts.source_locator: Krstić appeal, group destruction and targeting of men
facts.prompt: Why was the Srebrenica massacre recognized as genocide although the executions mainly targeted men and boys and women and children were expelled?
options: The killings were intended to destroy the Bosnian Muslim community of Srebrenica
The executions were classified as genocide because killing military-age prisoners is always genocide
The expulsion itself satisfied the destruction element, regardless of the purpose of the killings
The finding depended on an intention to kill all Bosnian Muslims throughout Bosnia
facts.explanation: The finding concerned intended destruction of a substantial part of the protected group. Sparing or expelling some members did not exclude it, and military age did not establish individual combatant status. This supplies a legal distinction, not an analogy proving Gaza has the same intent.
facts.source_name: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia — Krstić appeal summary
